## Initiative 86 Overview

Initiative 86 would ban force-feeding birds to enlarge their livers and prohibit the sale, distribution, and import of products resulting from it. The DC Board of Elections announced on August 5th that Initiative 86 officially qualified for the November 3rd, 2026 General Election Ballot, with Pro-Animal DC collecting 31,726 valid signatures—more than any other initiative in DC history.

## Poll Results

Nearly 8 in 10 DC voters support a law to end the sale of force-fed foie gras, according to a 2023 report published by DC Voter for Animals. Additionally, a majority of DC voters say they prefer to support restaurants that do not sell foie gras (61%).

## Current Campaign

Leading D.C. chefs have largely been mum about Initiative 86, but less than two weeks before local voters head to the polls, Chef José Andrés spoke out against the idea. A coalition of 100+ local restaurants, veterinarians, and animal rescues have endorsed Initiative 86.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Denver Initiated Ordinance 311 and foie gras in 2026:

## Overview

Initiated Ordinance 311 would prohibit the production and sale in the City and County of Denver of products made by force-feeding birds, including foie gras. If voters approve it, the restriction would take effect July 1, 2027.

## Key Details

Its restrictions would apply to producing and selling products made through force-feeding; foie gras produced without force-feeding would remain legal to sell. The principal effect would be on restaurants, which would have to remove items like foie gras from their menus. They could face fines of up to $5,000, or even lose city licenses, if they violated the ban.

## Ballot Status

Both cities will decide on November 3 whether to prohibit the sale of foie gras produced by force-feeding: Initiative 86 in DC and Initiated Ordinance 311 in Denver. Pro-Animal Colorado submitted more than 16,000 signatures to put the question on the ballot; just over 11,000 were deemed valid.

## Public Support

The campaign has cited Colorado State University polling showing that 85% of Colorado voters said they support ending the sale of foie gras produced using force-feeding methods.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about DC's Initiative 86 and the foie gras ban:

## Overview

District of Columbia voters will decide in November whether to outlaw the sale of foie gras produced through force-feeding, after the D.C. Board of Elections confirmed that Initiative Measure No. 86 gathered enough signatures to qualify for the ballot. Formally titled the Prohibiting the Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026, the measure targets duck and goose liver products made by inserting a tube down a bird's throat to deliver excessive feed.

## Signature Collection

Campaign circulators for Pro-Animal D.C. collected and submitted more than 45,000 voter signatures in 14 weeks, turning them in on July 6 — well beyond the 28,728 valid signatures the district requires. The petition drive was led by Pro-Animal D.C., a campaign of Pro-Animal Future, an animal welfare advocacy organization that promotes animal welfare laws through ballot initiatives.

## What the Ban Covers

The initiative bans only products resulting from forced feeding, meaning duck or goose livers harvested without that method would remain legal to sell and serve in District restaurants, which could give some vendors a path to keep liver dishes on the menu.

## Penalties and Related Litigation

If approved, Initiative 86 would prohibit the force-feeding of birds and ban the sale of products produced through that practice, including foie gras, with restaurants and businesses violating the law facing fines ranging from $1,000 to $5,000 and potentially having their business licenses suspended or revoked.

A lawsuit involving a Union Market butcher shop raised questions about the sale and labeling of duck livers marketed as foie gras.

Based on my search results, here's what I found about Initiative 86 and the opposition:

## Initiative 86 Overview

Initiative 86, formally known as the Prohibiting Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026, would prohibit the practice of force-feeding birds and ban the sale or distribution of any product resulting from force-feeding a bird, including foie gras.

## Restaurant Association Response

The Restaurant Association of Metropolitan Washington did not come out in full opposition. In a statement, RAMW said it "recognizes that people have differing views on foie gras, but a citywide ban is a significant response to a product served by a relatively small number of District restaurants." The group added that decisions about restaurant menus "are generally best left to individual businesses and the diners they serve," and said it hopes District voters "have clear information about what Initiative 86 would prohibit, how it would affect District restaurants, and whether a citywide ban is the right approach."

Notably, no formal opposition campaign has filed expense reports against the initiative. While some individual chefs like José Andrés have spoken out against the measure, the organized restaurant industry response has been notably restrained.

## Overview of the Ban

DC's Initiative 86, formally titled "Prohibiting the Force-Feeding of Birds Act of 2026," is focused on how the process to create foie gras affects animal welfare. Foie gras is the fattened liver from a force-fed goose or duck. It is produced by force-feeding ducks and geese to enlarge their livers.

## Legal Threats

Proceeds from the tasting menu will support a prospective "foie gras legal defense fund," as he's exploring legal challenges if the ban passes. ## House Status
The House passed the Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026 by a 224-200 vote in April, incorporating Section 12006, known as the Save Our Bacon Act. The provision would allow California to keep enforcing Proposition 12 within its own borders but would prohibit states from directly or indirectly enacting or enforcing livestock-production standards that reach beyond state lines.

## Senate Status
The Senate Agriculture Committee passed its version of the Farm Bill without the controversial Save Our Bacon Act on a party-line vote of 12-11 in September 2026. After significant opposition from stakeholders across the country, the bill does not include the harmful "Save Our Bacon Act" language that would have nullified California's Proposition 12, Massachusetts' Question 3, and other important state animal protection laws.

## Next Steps
If the Senate passes its version without the House provision, negotiators will have to reconcile the two bills and secure final approval before Congress could change Proposition 12's reach. A full Senate floor vote on the current agriculture package has not been scheduled.

As of October 6, 2026, prediction market traders price the odds of the Save Our Bacon Act preempting state animal welfare laws at just 5%, reflecting the split between the House's passage and the Senate Agriculture Committee's exclusion of the provision.

## Pro-Animal Future Activities

Pro Animal Future launched Measure 309 in Denver, which would prohibit the construction and operation of slaughterhouses within the city. However, Denver voters rejected two ballot measures seeking to prohibit slaughterhouses and fur products in the city.

Despite this setback, Pro-Animal Future spokesperson Olivia Hammond stated "We're in this for the long haul," and organizers intend to bring the issues to voters again in the future.

## Related 2028 Ballot Measures in Oregon and Colorado

Regarding statewide 2028 ballot plans:

**Oregon:** A measure to enshrine the right to hunt and fish within Oregon could be on the ballot in 2028, after clearing a procedural hurdle with enough signatures to go to the Oregon Attorney General.
